title: Design Autocomplete for Search
tagline: Show the best five suggestions after every keystroke, in under 100 milliseconds.

statement.prompt: Design the **autocomplete** (type-ahead) feature of a search engine. As a user types, show the most useful completions for what they have typed so far.
context: You are in a 45-minute interview. The interviewer gave you only the sentence above.
The product is already running a search engine. You are adding the suggestion box.
Think of typing `how t` and seeing `how to tie a tie`, `how to train your dragon`, `how to lose weight`.
given: About **10 million** users, each running about **10 searches a day**.
Each search triggers about **5 suggestion requests** while the user types.
There are about **100 million distinct queries** worth suggesting, around **30 bytes** each.

expectations.title: Drive the conversation
expectations.body: Ask questions before drawing anything. State your assumptions out loud so they can be corrected early.

expectations.title: Use numbers
expectations.body: Turn the givens into requests per second, storage and bandwidth. Every later choice should point back to one of them.

expectations.title: Start simple, then evolve
expectations.body: Get a working version on the board first. Add caches, sharding and queues only when a number or a requirement asks for them.

expectations.title: Go deep on the hard parts
expectations.body: For this problem the hard parts are choosing the data structure, keeping lookups in memory and refreshing popular queries without slowing reads.

expectations.title: Name the trade-offs
expectations.body: Say what you chose, what you gave up, and what would make you change your mind.

expectations.title: Think about failure
expectations.body: Point out single points of failure and say what happens when a node, a cache or a whole zone goes down.

scope_in: Returning ranked suggestions for a prefix
The data structure and how it is stored
Caching and scaling the read path
great: Chooses a **trie with top-k per node** and says why a SQL LIKE query fails.
Separates a **read-only serving path** from an **offline build path**.
Uses debounce and caching to cut load before it reaches the servers.

concepts.def: A tree where each step down adds one character. Every node represents a prefix, so all words under a node share it.
The k most popular results, pre-computed and stored at each node so a lookup does no ranking.
Wait for a short pause in typing before sending a request, so fast typists send one request instead of five.
New data shows up after a delay. Fine for suggestions, wrong for a bank balance.

numbers: 10M users x 10 searches x 5 keystrokes = **500M requests a day** = about **6,000/s**
Peak is usually **2 to 3 times** the average
Round a day to **86,400 seconds** (or about 100,000 for quick maths)

takeaways: Serve from an **in-memory trie with top-5 stored per node**, so a lookup costs the length of the prefix.
Keep the read path read-only; **rebuild the trie offline** from search logs and swap it in.
Cut load with **debounce, client caches and a prefix cache**; hot short prefixes are cheap to cache.
Suggestions are optional: **fail quietly** so search always works.

tradeoffs.cost: Suggestions lag by minutes or hours
Every replica holds the whole trie

extensions: Add a small real-time layer for trending queries
Personalise by mixing in the user's own recent searches
Filter offensive or banned suggestions before publishing

steps.title: What should autocomplete do?
steps.prompt: A user types into a search box. Which behaviours belong in the **core** scope? Select all that apply.
steps.hint: What is the smallest feature that still feels like autocomplete?
steps.explain: Core: **prefix match**, **top 5**, **ranked by popularity**, **reasonably fresh**. Spell correction and personalisation are extensions you name but do not build.

notes: Core: top 5 suggestions for a typed prefix, ranked by popularity
Out of scope: typo correction, personalisation

options.text: Match the prefix only, from the start of the query
options.why: Prefix matching keeps the problem tractable. Mid-word matching is an extension.

options.text: Suggestions update as search trends change
options.why: A stale list feels broken, so freshness matters, though not instantly.

options.text: Return the top 5 completions for the typed prefix
options.why: The heart of the feature.

options.text: Fix typos and understand meaning (spell correction, semantic search)
options.why: A separate, large problem. Mention it as a future extension.

options.text: A personal history for every user
options.why: Personalisation multiplies storage and is rarely core. Park it.

options.text: Rank suggestions by how often people search for them
options.why: Popularity is the simplest useful ranking.

steps.title: What qualities matter most?
steps.prompt: Pick the **non-functional** requirements that drive this design.
steps.hint: What does the user feel while typing?
steps.explain: **Speed** and **availability** over freshness. Say it out loud: *"stale by hours is fine, slow by 100 ms is not."*

notes: Latency under 100 ms; highly available; eventually consistent (hours old is fine)

options.text: High availability: search must work even if suggestions fail
options.why: Autocomplete is a helper. Failing quietly is better than breaking search.

options.text: Suggestions may be a few hours old (eventual consistency)
options.why: Nobody needs the last minute's searches in the list. This relaxation makes the design far easier.

options.text: Perfect accuracy of every suggestion
options.why: Approximate popularity is fine.

options.text: Very low latency: suggestions in under 100 ms
options.why: Suggestions that arrive after the user finishes typing are useless.

options.text: Strong consistency: every new search appears in suggestions instantly
options.why: Costly and pointless here.

steps.title: How many suggestion requests per second?
steps.prompt: There are **10 million** users. Each does about **10 searches a day** and every search fires about **5 suggestion requests** (one per keystroke after a short pause). What is the average **requests per second**?
steps.hint: Requests per day divided by about 86,000.
steps.explain: About **6,000 per second, 15,000 at peak**. Far too much to run a database query per keystroke, so lookups must come from **memory**, and most from a **cache**.

notes: Load: about 6,000 requests/s average, about 15,000/s peak

work: 10,000,000 users x 10 searches = 100,000,000 searches a day
Peak is 2 to 3 times: plan for about **15,000 per second**

steps.title: How much data is the dictionary?
steps.prompt: You keep **100 million distinct queries**, about **30 bytes** each. How many **GB** is the raw text?
steps.explain: Raw text is only **3 GB**; the trie with its top-k lists is a few tens of GB. That fits in the memory of **one large machine**, so the problem is serving *speed*, not data size. We replicate for traffic, not for capacity.

notes: Data: about 3 GB of query text, 15-30 GB as an in-memory trie

work: A trie shares common prefixes and stores top-5 lists per node, so budget about 5 to 10 times more: **15 to 30 GB**

steps.title: How do we store the suggestions?
steps.prompt: A user types `ho`. Which structure returns the best 5 completions quickest?
steps.hint: Move the work from query time to build time.
steps.explain: Store **top-k inside each node**. Lookup time depends only on the prefix length, which is tiny. You trade extra memory for constant-time answers.

notes: Structure: trie, each node stores its top 5 suggestions

steps.pitfall: Querying the database with LIKE on every keystroke.
steps.followup: How much memory does storing top-5 at every node cost, and how can you reduce it?

options.text: A trie where every node stores the pre-computed top 5 for its prefix
options.why: Walking `h` then `o` takes 2 steps and the answer is already sitting in the node.

options.text: A SQL table queried with `WHERE query LIKE 'ho%' ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT 5`
options.why: Scans and sorts many rows per keystroke. At 15,000 requests per second it collapses.

options.text: A trie without top-k, collecting and sorting the whole subtree at query time
options.why: Short prefixes like `a` have millions of descendants. Far too slow.

options.text: A sorted list of all queries and a binary search
options.why: Finds the start of the range but still has to rank everything in it.

steps.title: What should the browser do?
steps.prompt: The API is `GET /suggest?q=ho`. Which client behaviours keep the load down and the UI snappy?
steps.hint: Make the user's browser do some of the work.
steps.explain: Client-side tricks are free scaling: **debounce, cancel stale requests, cache locally**. Mention them early, interviewers like it.

notes: API: GET /suggest?q=prefix -> 5 strings. Client debounces, cancels stale calls, caches

options.text: **Debounce**: wait about 100-200 ms after the last keystroke before sending
options.why: Cuts requests a lot, because people type several characters quickly.

options.text: Download the whole dictionary to the browser
options.why: Gigabytes. Not an option.

options.text: Cache answers for prefixes already seen in this session
options.why: Backspacing re-uses answers for free.

options.text: Cancel the previous request when a new character arrives
options.why: A slow old answer must not overwrite a fresh one.

options.text: Send a request on every single keystroke with no delay
options.why: Triples the load for no gain.

steps.title: Trace one request
steps.prompt: The user has typed `ho`. Put the steps of the **read path** in order, first at the top.
steps.hint: Cheapest check first, most expensive last.
steps.explain: A **cache in front of an in-memory trie**. Both answer in microseconds, so the network is the slowest part.

notes: Read path: browser -> suggestion service -> prefix cache -> trie

items.text: Browser waits for a short pause, then sends `GET /suggest?q=ho`
items.why: Debounce first so you only send useful requests.

items.text: Suggestion service looks in the prefix cache
items.why: Short prefixes are extremely hot, so most requests end here.

items.text: On a miss, the service reads the node for `ho` in the in-memory trie
items.why: A few pointer hops. No disk, no database.

items.text: The service stores the answer in the prefix cache
items.why: The next person typing `ho` gets a cache hit.

items.text: The top 5 suggestions are returned to the browser
items.why: Total time: a few milliseconds plus network.

steps.title: How does the trie stay fresh?
steps.prompt: Searches happen all day. Which pieces form the **write path** (the data pipeline)?
steps.hint: Reads must never wait for writes.
steps.explain: Keep the **read path read-only** and rebuild **offline**. Servers load the new trie and swap a pointer. If a build fails, the old trie keeps serving.

notes: Write path: search logs -> aggregator -> trie builder -> publish new trie (hourly or daily)

steps.followup: How would you surface a sudden trending topic within minutes?

options.text: Ask the user to refresh the dictionary manually
options.why: Not a system.

options.text: Update the live trie in place on every search
options.why: A write on every search fights with 15,000 reads per second and needs locking.

options.text: An aggregator that counts queries per day or week
options.why: Batch counting is cheap and reliable.

options.text: A builder that creates a new trie from the counts and publishes it
options.why: Build offline, then swap, so reads never see a half-built trie.

options.text: Log every completed search query
options.why: The raw material for popularity counts.

steps.title: How do we scale beyond one machine?
steps.prompt: Traffic is 15,000 requests per second and the trie is 30 GB. What is the best way to scale?
steps.hint: Is it a size problem or a request-rate problem?
steps.explain: Scale in the order the numbers say: **replicas first** (traffic), **prefix-range shards** later (memory). If you shard, split by observed traffic because `s` is far busier than `x`.

notes: Scale: replicate the trie across servers; shard by prefix range only when memory needs it

steps.pitfall: Sharding the trie when it fits in memory on one machine.
steps.followup: You do shard by first letter. Which shard gets overloaded and what do you do?

options.text: Replicate the whole trie on many servers behind a load balancer; add range shards by prefix only if memory becomes a limit
options.why: The trie fits in memory, so the bottleneck is request rate. Replicas fix that simply.

options.text: Run one huge server and scale it vertically
options.why: A single point of failure and a ceiling.

options.text: Move the trie into a relational database with an index
options.why: Slower than memory, harder to keep top-k.

options.text: Shard by hash of the prefix so every prefix lands somewhere random
options.why: Works, but the benefit is memory, which is not our problem, and a suggestion service now needs many hops.

steps.title: What if something fails?
steps.prompt: Which measures keep suggestions working through failures?
steps.hint: Which part is allowed to fail without anyone noticing?
steps.explain: Autocomplete is **optional for the user**, so degrade quietly. Protect the swap of data with a **validate then switch** step.

notes: Failure: multi-zone replicas, fail open (search works without suggestions), validated trie swaps, CDN for hot prefixes

options.text: Rate limit the endpoint and add a CDN for the hottest prefixes
options.why: Protects the service and shaves most traffic.

options.text: Several suggestion servers across zones behind a load balancer
options.why: No single point of failure.

options.text: Keep the previous trie version and roll back if a new build looks wrong
options.why: Validate size and a sample of queries before swapping.

options.text: If suggestions fail or time out, the search box still works without them
options.why: Graceful degradation: the helper may fail, the product may not.

options.text: Block the search page until suggestions load
options.why: Turns a nice-to-have into an outage.

steps.title: Defend your design
steps.prompt: In two or three sentences: what did you trade away, and what would make you change the design?
steps.explain: Say the trade-off as **"I chose X over Y because of Z"**. It shows judgement, which is what the interview scores.

notes: Trade-offs: freshness vs latency, memory vs query-time work

steps.model: I traded **freshness** for **speed**: the trie is rebuilt offline, so new trends appear after minutes or hours, but reads are served from memory in milliseconds. I spent **memory** (top-5 stored in each node) to avoid doing any ranking at query time. I would move to a real-time layer if product needed trending topics within minutes, and shard by prefix range if the dictionary outgrew one machine.
points: Named the trade-off: freshness vs latency
Memory (top-k per node) bought constant-time lookups
Offline build keeps the read path simple and safe
Said what would change the design (trending topics, dictionary growth)
